Woodrow Wilson. The 28th president of the United States, serving from 1913 to 1921. A Democrat and former president of Princeton University, Wilson led America through World War One and its aftermath, championing the principle of national self-determination and the creation of the League of Nations. His domestic agenda, the New Freedom, sought to restore competition and reduce corporate monopolies. Though idealistic in his foreign policy vision, his presidency ended amid the League's rejection and a personal stroke.

Wilson won the 1912 election as a Progressive, splitting the Republican vote between himself and Theodore Roosevelt. He governed with a coalition of Southern Democrats and reformers.

He passed landmark domestic legislation including the Federal Reserve Act in 1913, the Clayton Antitrust Act, and the 16th Amendment establishing the income tax. He campaigned for reelection in 1916 on the slogan "He kept us out of war," but declared war on Germany in April 1917 after unrestricted submarine warfare threatened American vessels and lives.

He articulated the Fourteen Points in 1918, outlining his vision for a just postwar order based on open covenants, national self-determination, and a League of Nations. He negotiated the Treaty of Versailles in 1919 and embedded the League of Nations covenant within it. However, the Republican-controlled Senate rejected the treaty, dealing Wilson a devastating political defeat.

He suffered a severe stroke in October 1919 while touring America to promote the League. He spent his final eighteen months largely incapacitated, with his wife and cabinet managing his duties.
